questions.stem: Which adage from the Mahābhārata is inscribed on the emblem of the Supreme Court of India?
stem_variants: What Mahābhārata motto is featured on the Supreme Court of India's crest?
questions.answer: Yato dharmas tato jayaḥ
questions.explanation: 'Yato dharmas tato jayaḥ' (Where there is Dharma, there is victory) is the foundational refrain of the Mahābhārata and is inscribed on the official insignia of the Supreme Court of India.
questions.source_quote: It is inscribed on the Supreme Court of India's emblem...

questions.stem: Under what specific circumstance did Yudhiṣṭhira utter the maxim 'Vayaṃ pañcādhikaṃ śatam' (We are one hundred and five)?
stem_variants: In which episode did Yudhiṣṭhira instruct his brothers that Kurus are 105 against external adversaries?
options: When Duryodhana was captured by the Gandharvas during the Pāṇḍavas' forest exile
During the peace embassy of Sañjaya prior to the Kurukṣetra war
When Jayadratha abducted Draupadī in the Kāmyaka forest
During the cattle raid of Virāṭa by the Trigartas and Kauravas
distractor_pool: During the peace embassy of Sañjaya prior to the Kurukṣetra war
When Jayadratha abducted Draupadī in the Kāmyaka forest
During the cattle raid of Virāṭa by the Trigartas and Kauravas
questions.answer: When Duryodhana was captured by the Gandharvas during the Pāṇḍavas' forest exile
accepted_answers: When Duryodhana was captured by the Gandharvas during the Pāṇḍavas' forest exile
questions.explanation: When the Gandharva king Citrasena captured Duryodhana in the Dvaita forest, Bhīma felt relieved, but Yudhiṣṭhira commanded them to rescue him, stating that while they fight each other as 5 and 100, against an outsider they are 105.
questions.source_quote: When the Gandharvas captured Duryodhana during exile, Yudhiṣṭhira told Bhīma and Arjuna to free him...

questions.stem: According to the subhāṣita illustrating 'Ati sarvatra varjayet', which three vices/virtues led respectively to the downfall of Karṇa, Suyodhana (Duryodhana), and Daśagrīva (Rāvaṇa)?
stem_variants: What respective excesses caused the destruction of Karṇa, Duryodhana, and Rāvaṇa in the traditional verse?
options: Ati-dāna (excessive charity), Ati-lobha (excessive greed), and Ati-kāma (excessive lust)
Ati-krodha (excessive wrath), Ati-māna (excessive pride), and Ati-lobha (excessive greed)
Ati-dāna (excessive charity), Ati-ahaṃkāra (excessive ego), and Ati-moha (excessive delusion)
Ati-bhakti (excessive devotion), Ati-lobha (excessive greed), and Ati-mada (excessive arrogance)
distractor_pool: Ati-krodha (excessive wrath), Ati-māna (excessive pride), and Ati-lobha (excessive greed)
Ati-dāna (excessive charity), Ati-ahaṃkāra (excessive ego), and Ati-moha (excessive delusion)
Ati-bhakti (excessive devotion), Ati-lobha (excessive greed), and Ati-mada (excessive arrogance)
questions.answer: Ati-dāna (excessive charity), Ati-lobha (excessive greed), and Ati-kāma (excessive lust)
accepted_answers: Ati-dāna (excessive charity), Ati-lobha (excessive greed), and Ati-kāma (excessive lust)
questions.explanation: The subhāṣita explicitly states: 'atidānād hataḥ Karṇaḥ atilobhāt Suyodhanaḥ, atikāmād Daśagrīvaḥ, ati sarvatra varjayet'—Karṇa fell through disproportionate charity, Duryodhana through uncontrolled greed, and Rāvaṇa through unchecked carnal desire.
questions.source_quote: atidānād hataḥ Karṇaḥ atilobhāt Suyodhanaḥ, atikāmād Daśagrīvaḥ, ati sarvatra varjayet

questions.stem: In the Yakṣa Praśna, why does Yudhiṣṭhira argue that the path of the 'Mahājana' must be followed rather than relying exclusively on logic (tarka) or scriptural texts (śruti)?
stem_variants: What epistemological limitation of tarka and śruti does Yudhiṣṭhira point out in Vana Parva?
options: Logic is inconclusive (apratiṣṭha) and śrutis offer diverse, contextual perspectives without a single universally accepted sage
Logic is entirely unholy while revealed texts have been corrupted across yugas
Logic is subordinate to royal decrees, and śrutis are reserved exclusively for sannyāsins
The Vedas explicitly forbid the application of rational inquiry to moral dilemmas
distractor_pool: Logic is entirely unholy while revealed texts have been corrupted across yugas
Logic is subordinate to royal decrees, and śrutis are reserved exclusively for sannyāsins
The Vedas explicitly forbid the application of rational inquiry to moral dilemmas
questions.answer: Logic is inconclusive (apratiṣṭha) and śrutis offer diverse, contextual perspectives without a single universally accepted sage
accepted_answers: Logic is inconclusive (apratiṣṭha) and śrutis offer diverse, contextual perspectives without a single universally accepted sage
questions.explanation: The verse notes 'tarko 'pratiṣṭhaḥ śrutayo vibhinnā nāsāv ṛṣir yasya mataṃ na bhinnam'—reasoning is without final grounding because an intellect can always overturn another's argument, scriptures offer multifaceted prescriptions, and sages disagree; thus, the core of dharma is concealed and best illuminated by the conduct of great beings.
questions.source_quote: Logic alone cannot fix dharma's subtle principle (one would just follow the cleverest); the śrutis differ and are contextual...

questions.stem: Which Mahābhārata narrative directly serves as the origin of the 'Sundopasunda Nyāya', and what philosophical/strategic maxim does it represent?
stem_variants: What is the source narrative and metaphorical meaning of Sundopasunda Nyāya?
options: The Ādi Parva tale of two mutually attached asura brothers who destroyed one another over the apsaras Tilottamā; representing mutual annihilation
The Sabhā Parva contest between Jarāsandha and Bhīma; representing combat between equals resulting in exhaustion
The Udyoga Parva debate between Karṇa and Śalya; representing internal sabotage within an alliance
The Śānti Parva parable of the cat and the mouse; representing temporary pragmatic coalitions between sworn enemies
distractor_pool: The Sabhā Parva contest between Jarāsandha and Bhīma; representing combat between equals resulting in exhaustion
The Udyoga Parva debate between Karṇa and Śalya; representing internal sabotage within an alliance
The Śānti Parva parable of the cat and the mouse; representing temporary pragmatic coalitions between sworn enemies
questions.answer: The Ādi Parva tale of two mutually attached asura brothers who destroyed one another over the apsaras Tilottamā; representing mutual annihilation
accepted_answers: The Ādi Parva tale of two mutually attached asura brothers who destroyed one another over the apsaras Tilottamā; representing mutual annihilation
questions.explanation: Sundopasunda Nyāya derives from chapters 209-212 of the Ādi Parva, where the invincible asura brothers Sunda and Upasunda turn upon each other and cause their own mutual destruction when infatuated with the apsaras Tilottamā, created by Viśvakarmā at Brahmā's direction.
questions.source_quote: Sundopasunda Nyāya: mutual destruction; source is Ādi Parva chapters 209-212: the invincible asura brothers Sunda and Upasunda conquered three worlds; Brahmā had Viśvakarmā create the apsaras Tilottamā...
